overview.title: 📖 Overview: Signs, Minorities, and a Goat's Triplets
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 20a–20b
overview.hebrewSource: עֵז שֶׁטִּינְּפָה בַּת שִׁשָּׁה — יוֹלֶדֶת בְּתוֹךְ שְׁנָתָהּ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues analyzing when the offspring of a gentile-purchased animal is certainly, or only uncertainly, a firstborn. Rava and Ravina each explain why Rabbi Yishmael's age-based rule doesn't simply follow the statistical majority of animals that give birth within a year. Rabbi Yehoshua then corrects Rabbi Yishmael in the name of the Rabbis: an unseen murky discharge (טִינּוּף) can also indicate a prior pregnancy, and the Gemara works through three separate technical explanations — involving Ze'eiri's thirty-day rule, premature birth, and whether part of a day counts as a full day — for why Rabbi Yehoshua's own position is more lenient than the view he transmits. A parallel dispute follows over whether producing milk alone, without a discharge, exempts the next offspring, complete with a baraita that reverses who says what. The daf closes with a puzzle about a kid and her triplet daughters reaching the animal-tithe quota, revealing along the way that an animal does not give birth twice within a single year.

slides.title: ⚖️ Which Majority Counts?
slides.subtitle: Why doesn't Rabbi Yishmael's rule simply follow 'most animals give birth within a year'?

boxes.title: Rava's Explanation
items: Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Meir's principle: one must be concerned for the minority (חוֹשְׁשִׁין לְמִיעוּטָא)
So the statistical majority of animals that give birth within a year does not remove the doubt

boxes.title: Ravina's Explanation
items: Even the Rabbis, who normally do follow a majority, agree here
This majority is action-dependent (תָּלוּי בְּמַעֲשֶׂה) — whether the animal mated at all — not a fixed feature of reality
An action-dependent majority is not followed, unlike an examinable majority such as nine kosher shops

callout.label: Shared conclusion:
callout.text: Both explanations preserve Rabbi Yishmael's uncertainty rule without forcing him to adopt Rabbi Meir's general concern for minorities.

slides.title: 🐐 Does a Hidden Discharge Still Exempt the Offspring?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehoshua, in the name of the Rabbis, corrects Rabbi Yishmael's age-based certainty

nodes.content: ❓ A murky discharge (טִינּוּף) is a sign of a completed pregnancy. But what if no one actually saw one?
✅ Everyone agrees: if a discharge is seen, it exempts the next offspring from firstborn status

columns.label: Rabbi Yishmael
columns.content: Not concerned about an unseen discharge — assume none occurred, so the age-based rule stands

columns.label: Rabbi Yehoshua
columns.content: Concerned even for an unseen discharge — the next offspring remains uncertain

nodes.content: 🔑 Rava's resolution: Rabbi Yishmael is concerned for the minority — but only when it leads to a stringency (giving to the priest), never to a leniency (freeing the owner)

callout.label: Alternative:
callout.text: Or they disagree over whether a discharging animal can return to fertility and give birth within the same year at all.

slides.title: 📅 Three Ways to Explain Rabbi Yehoshua's Own Leniency
slides.subtitle: Both his transmitted 'Rabbis' opinion and his own view agree a discharge doesn't rule out a same-year birth — so what's the practical difference?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Case: a goat discharges at six months, then gives birth before its first year ends

2️⃣ Answer 1 — Ze'eiri's rule: a real discharge blocks pregnancy for 30 days. The transmitted 'Rabbis' view accepts this (so a birth within a month proves it wasn't a real discharge); Rabbi Yehoshua's own view rejects Ze'eiri entirely
3️⃣ Answer 2 — Can an animal give birth prematurely (מְקוּטָּעִין)? The transmitted view says no; Rabbi Yehoshua's own view says yes, allowing a shorter pregnancy after the discharge
4️⃣ Answer 3 — Is part of a day counted as a full day (מִקְצָת הַיּוֹם כְּכוּלּוֹ)? Rabbi Yehoshua's own view says yes, letting pregnancy begin on day 30; the transmitted view says no

callout.label: Why three answers?
callout.text: Each 'if you wish, say instead' (וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא) offers an independent way to locate the real practical gap — the Gemara leaves all three live.

slides.title: 🥛 Does Milk Alone Exempt the Next Offspring?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥanina of Sura finds a practical difference between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehoshua — with a twist

lines.speaker: R' Ḥanina
lines.text: There is a difference: an animal that already produces milk, with no discharge seen at all.

lines.speaker: R' Akiva
lines.text: Milk exempts the offspring — follow the majority of animals, and most do not produce milk unless they have given birth.

lines.speaker: R' Yehoshua
lines.text: A minority of animals do produce milk without having given birth — so the next offspring stays uncertain.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But does Rabbi Yehoshua really worry about a minority? A mishna rules a widow need not worry her late mother-in-law bore a levir, even though a minority of pregnancies could yield one!

lines.speaker: Correction
lines.text: Rather, reverse the two opinions. A baraita confirms it: Rabbi Yehoshua says milk does exempt; Rabbi Akiva says it does not.

callout.label: Lesson:
callout.text: Attributions transmitted through intermediate reports can be reversed once a direct baraita is found — the Gemara trusts the more direct source.

slides.title: 🐑 A Kid, Her Daughters, and the Tithe Pen
slides.subtitle: A baraita's numbers reveal an unstated halakha
rows: A kid bears triplet daughters, and each daughter also bears triplets
Mother + 3 daughters + 9 granddaughters = 13 animals, all entering the pen to be tithed within one year
Why does every daughter bear exactly three, not a mix of two and three?
One daughter alone cannot reach the ten-animal quota with the mother unless she bears three — the baraita states three for all, for consistency
Why not instead have the daughters bear two each, and let the original mother give birth again alongside them?
That route is never proposed — implying the halakha that a goat does not give birth twice within the same year
He personally saw a single kid whose descendants reached the tithe quota within its very first year

callout.label: Hidden principle:
callout.text: The baraita's silence about a repeat birth from the same mother is itself evidence that a goat cannot give birth a second time within one year.

summary.principle: An animal's firstborn status stays uncertain whenever a possible sign of a prior birth — a discharge, milk, or simple statistics — cannot be ruled out, and every leniency Rabbi Yehoshua grants can be independently explained through timing rules the Gemara leaves open.

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ Rava and Ravina explain why Rabbi Yishmael's age rule resists the statistical majority of same-year births
🐐 Rabbi Yehoshua: even an unseen discharge must be considered — Rava limits Rabbi Yishmael's concern to stringencies only
📅 Three technical explanations (30-day rule, premature birth, part-day-as-whole) locate the real gap between Rabbi Yehoshua's transmitted and personal views

columns.content: 🥛 Milk alone: Rabbi Yehoshua exempts, Rabbi Akiva does not (baraita corrects the reported order)
🐑 The triplets baraita implies a goat cannot give birth twice in one year

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Only a real, examinable sign — seen or reliably inferred — removes the uncertainty that firstborn status depends on

quiz.q: According to Ravina, why don't the Rabbis follow the statistical majority that most animals give birth within their first year?
o: Because that majority is action-dependent, not a fixed feature of reality, and such majorities are not followed
Because the Rabbis reject the concept of majority entirely
Because animals in Eretz Yisrael behave differently
Because Rabbi Yishmael personally rejected majorities
quiz.e: Ravina explains that the Rabbis only follow an examinable majority (like most shops selling kosher meat), not a majority that depends on an action such as whether an animal mated — so this statistical claim doesn't override the uncertainty.

quiz.q: According to Rava, when is Rabbi Yishmael concerned for the minority possibility of a hidden discharge?
o: Only when it would create a stringency, never a leniency
Only when it would create a leniency, never a stringency
In every case, without exception
Never, under any circumstances
quiz.e: Rava resolves the apparent inconsistency by saying Rabbi Yishmael is concerned for the minority only when that concern leads to a stringent outcome (giving the animal to the priest), not when it would lead to a leniency for the owner.

quiz.q: In the third explanation of Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency, what does his own opinion hold about 'part of a day' (מִקְצָת הַיּוֹם כְּכוּלוֹ)?
o: Part of a day is never counted as a whole day
Part of a day counts as a whole day, allowing pregnancy to begin as early as day thirty after the discharge
The concept is irrelevant to animal pregnancy
Only human pregnancies use this principle
quiz.e: According to this explanation, Rabbi Yehoshua's own view holds that part of a day counts as an entire day, so the goat could have become pregnant on the thirtieth day after the discharge and still give birth just before the year's end.

quiz.q: According to the baraita that reverses the earlier attribution, who holds that milk production alone exempts the next offspring from firstborn status?
o: Rabbi Akiva
Rabbi Yehoshua
Rabbi Yishmael
Rabbi Shimon
quiz.e: The Gemara corrects the initial attribution: a baraita teaches that it is Rabbi Yehoshua who says milk production exempts the offspring, while Rabbi Akiva says it does not.

quiz.q: What unstated halakha does the Gemara derive from the baraita's insistence that all three daughter-goats, not just one, bear triplets?
o: That goats always give birth to triplets
That a goat cannot give birth twice within the same year
That triplets are never subject to the animal tithe
That Rabbi Shimon disputes the entire baraita
quiz.e: The Gemara notes that the baraita never proposes having the original mother give birth again alongside her granddaughters to reach the tithe quota — implying that a goat does not give birth a second time within a single year.
